active_paradigms.idea: Greedy per-row online Trie construction: choose each row's column order to maximize prefix reuse against already-committed rows
active_paradigms.description: Exploit the fact that the Trie objective rewards long shared prefixes, and that per-row column orders are allowed to differ. Build the output incrementally: maintain the set of already-emitted serialized strings (as a sorted list for LCP lookup). For each next row, evaluate 2-4 candidate column orderings for that row (generated from column repetition statistics restricted to not-yet-placed columns) and pick the ordering whose serialized string has the maximum LCP against the current sorted set (findable via bisect on the sorted list plus checking the two neighbors). Insert the chosen string and proceed. This directly optimizes the actual character-prefix objective per row instead of relying on global statistics, and it lets rows that share a long common value in an unusual column reorder to expose that value first. Rows should be processed in an order that groups similar rows (e.g., pre-sorted by the global candidate string) so neighbors in the insertion stream share content. Score the final multiset with the exact sorted-LCP objective and keep the better of this construction and the current best candidate.
active_paradigms.what_to_optimize: Primary hit rate (matched characters) on datasets like PDMX and BIRD where row-specific reordering can expose shared long values that any single global column order hides.
active_paradigms.cautions: Candidate generation must be bounded (e.g., 3-4 orderings per row, top-ranked by the cheap count*(count-1)*len statistic restricted to unplaced columns). Never modify cell values. Keep total runtime under the 12s average budget by capping rows processed in the greedy pass and falling back to the current best candidate for the rest. Use the existing binary-search LCP for scoring, not per-character loops.
active_paradigms.approach_type: greedy trie-insertion with per-row column reordering

active_paradigms.idea: Exact-objective local search: iterative column-position refinement scored by the true sorted-LCP Trie objective
active_paradigms.description: Treat the problem as choosing, per row, a permutation of columns so that the multiset of serialized strings has minimal total distinct-prefix cost (equivalently maximal adjacent-LCP sum after sorting). Start from the best existing candidate ordering. Then iterate a coordinate-descent refinement: for each column position p (bounded sweep, 2-3 passes), consider moving that column earlier or later within each row's ordering, recompute the row's serialized string, sort all strings, and accept the move if the exact LCP-sum score improves. Because the LCP-sum for a fixed multiset is order-independent, each evaluation is one sort plus one linear LCP pass using the existing C-speed binary-search LCP, so a full sweep over columns costs roughly n_cols sorts — acceptable for these table sizes. Use lexicographic tie-breaking (numpy argsort on string arrays) to keep results deterministic. This escapes local optima of the conditional-tree constructions by letting the true objective drive every decision, and it naturally produces row-specific orders (rows in different tree leaves get different optimal moves).
active_paradigms.what_to_optimize: Hit rate improvements on all five datasets, especially movies/products where long text fields (titles, bodies) dominate and small position changes yield large character savings; also runtime efficiency via vectorized string joins per candidate pass.
active_paradigms.cautions: Only move whole columns per row; never split a column's values. The merged-column blocks must be kept contiguous in the emitted orderings per existing API semantics. Bound iterations to 2-3 full passes over columns; each pass is O(n_cols * sort) which is cheap. Verify the final candidate with the exact LCP score before emitting.
active_paradigms.approach_type: suffix-array style lexicographic refinement of column orders

active_paradigms.idea: Prefix-block alignment: exploit col_merge structure and value-factorized grouping to align identical long values at identical string offsets
active_paradigms.description: Reformulate the construction around contiguous blocks of columns rather than individual columns. First, honor col_merge by keeping each merge group as one atomic block (concatenating their serialized values when scoring). Second, discover additional implicit blocks: columns whose values co-occur (e.g., via a cheap dependency check — for each pair of columns with low distinct counts, compare factorized code arrays with numpy array equality; also detect constant or near-constant columns). Build a small set of candidate block orders: (i) the current global frequency-ranked order, (ii) an order that places all low-cardinality/high-repetition blocks first so rows share long categorical prefixes, then long free-text blocks last, (iii) the reverse for datasets where free text has heavy n-gram overlap (detected by sampling LCPs of raw text values). Use pandas factorize once per column for integer codes, numpy bincount for repetition statistics, and score each whole candidate with the exact sorted-LCP sum, returning the best. This differs from the current tree approach because it optimizes block placement globally with the true objective rather than greedily partitioning rows, and it exploits the evaluator's cross-field prefix matching (a match may end inside a field, so putting a long shared text field right after a shared categorical prefix captures partial-field reuse).
active_paradigms.what_to_optimize: Hit rate via better cross-field and partial-field prefix capture (the evaluator counts matches ending inside a field), plus runtime via one-time factorization and vectorized statistics.
active_paradigms.cautions: Merged-column groups must stay contiguous and in API-mandated order within each row's ordering. Ensure object-dtype output preserves exact original values (including NaN sentinels serialized as ''). Keep the number of candidate block orders bounded (e.g., top-3 by the pair-repetition score) and score each once with the exact LCP objective, never inside the grouping loop.
active_paradigms.approach_type: pandas groupby + numpy bincount block alignment
